name: Koshari
clues: It is a colonial accident: three continents' pantries collided in one bowl and nobody thought to separate them again.
Sold from tiled shopfronts along the Nile for a handful of coins, and eaten standing up with a tin of vinegar on the counter.
Starch upon starch — small pasta, grains and two kinds of pulse in one heap, crowned with something crisp and sweet.
Egypt's national street dish: lentils, rice and macaroni under spiced tomato sauce, garlic vinegar and fried onions.
fact: It emerged in the nineteenth century, blending Indian lentil-and-rice traditions brought by British troops with Italian pasta.

name: Molokhia
clues: A Fatimid caliph is said to have banned it outright, which only made people want it more.
The final garlic tempering is poured in hissing, and cooks say the sound itself is part of the recipe.
Finely minced green leaves that thicken the broth to something viscous and rope-like, poured over rice.
The Egyptian soup of chopped jute mallow leaves in chicken broth, finished with a hiss of fried garlic and coriander.
fact: The mucilaginous texture divides people completely; boiling it too long destroys both the colour and the viscosity.

name: Ful Medames
clues: Traces of it have been found in pharaonic tombs, and the second half of its name refers to the buried pot it cooked in.
It is the breakfast of the working morning across the Nile valley and the Levant, ladled from a bulbous copper vessel.
Brown beans stewed overnight and crushed at the table with oil, lemon and a heavy hand of cumin.
Egypt's slow-cooked fava bean breakfast, mashed with olive oil, garlic and lemon and scooped with flatbread.
fact: The traditional vessel, a qidra, is a narrow-necked pot set into embers so the beans cook overnight without boiling dry.

name: Harira
clues: During one month of the year it is the first thing to touch the lips at sunset, eaten with dates and a honeyed pastry.
It is thickened at the very end with a fermented flour-and-water mixture whisked in as the pot boils.
A cloudy tomato-based broth thick with two pulses and fine pasta, sharp with celery leaf and coriander.
Morocco's Ramadan soup of chickpeas, lentils and lamb, thickened with a flour slurry and finished with lemon.
fact: The thickener, tadouira, is flour and water left to sour for a day or two, which adds a subtle tang as well as body.

name: Bastilla
clues: Its name descends from the Spanish word for a small pie, carried across the strait by Andalusian exiles.
It is the show-stopper of the Fez wedding table, dusted in a pattern before it reaches the guests.
Layers of tissue-thin pastry over shredded poultry, a lemony egg curd and ground nuts — then sugar and cinnamon on top.
The Moroccan sweet-savoury pie of pigeon or chicken in paper-thin warqa, finished with icing sugar and cinnamon.
fact: Warqa is not filo — it is dabbed onto a hot dome in overlapping circles rather than rolled and stretched.

name: Zaalouk
clues: It belongs to a family of small cooked salads that arrive together at the start of a meal, a dozen little dishes at once.
In Morocco it is one of the standard kemia, scooped up with bread before anything else appears.
A soft, almost jammy purée of charred nightshades cooked down with garlic and sweet paprika until the oil separates.
The Moroccan cooked salad of smoky mashed aubergine and tomato, served cool with bread.
fact: The aubergine is usually grilled or roasted whole first, so the smoke goes into the flesh before it is ever mashed.

name: Ghormeh Sabzi
clues: The herbs must be fried until they turn almost black, and rushing that step is the classic beginner's mistake.
It is routinely voted the national dish of its country, and diaspora families judge each other by it.
A very dark green stew, sour rather than spicy, with beans and lamb, punctured by whole shrivelled citrus.
Iran's herb stew of parsley and fenugreek with dried limes and kidney beans, served over saffron rice.
fact: The sourness comes from limu omani — limes boiled in brine and sun-dried until hollow, pierced before going into the pot.

name: Fesenjan
clues: Its two defining ingredients both appear on the reliefs of Persepolis, and it may be one of the oldest stews still cooked.
It belongs to the Caspian north, and the winter solstice table, where duck is the traditional protein.
A thick sauce that darkens from beige to near-black as ground nuts release their oil, balanced sweet against sharply sour.
The Iranian stew of ground walnuts and pomegranate molasses, usually with chicken or duck, over rice.
fact: The colour change is the doneness test — the walnut oil must separate and the sauce must go glossy and almost black.

name: Ash Reshteh
clues: The noodles in it are symbolic: pulling strands is associated with untangling the threads of one's fate.
It is cooked for Nowruz and for charitable vows, in cauldrons big enough to feed a whole street.
A thick green pottage of pulses and herbs with flat wheat strands, swirled with a sour whey and dark fried mint.
The Persian new year soup of noodles, beans and herbs, topped with fermented whey, crisp onion and mint oil.
fact: Kashk, the drizzle on top, is drained fermented whey — sharp and salty, and quite unlike yogurt or sour cream.

name: Tahchin
clues: Its name means arranged at the bottom, and the bottom is precisely the part everyone fights over.
It is turned out of the dish upside down at the table, and a crack in the crust is a small domestic tragedy.
Grains bound with yogurt and yolk, baked until the base sets into a burnished golden shell around a soft interior.
The Iranian saffron rice cake layered with chicken and barberries, inverted to show its crisp crust.
fact: The prized bottom crust belongs to the wider tahdig tradition, but here yogurt and egg yolk make it a solid, sliceable layer.

name: Mansaf
clues: It is eaten standing, with the right hand only, from a communal tray, and the guest of honour is handed the head.
The sauce depends on hard discs of dried, salted, fermented sheep's milk that must be soaked back to life.
Lamb poached in a tart white dairy broth over rice and a layer of thin bread, scattered with toasted nuts.
Jordan's national dish: lamb cooked in fermented dried yogurt, served over rice and flatbread.
fact: Jameed is sun-dried fermented ewe's milk pressed into rock-hard balls, and its sourness is the whole point of the dish.

name: Maqluba
clues: Its name is a warning about how it is served: the pot goes over, and everyone holds their breath.
A thirteenth-century Baghdadi cookbook already describes something very like it.
Fried vegetables lining the base of the pot become the top of a moulded tower of spiced rice and meat.
The Palestinian upside-down pot of rice layered with fried aubergine, cauliflower and chicken.
fact: The layering order is reversed deliberately, so the browned aubergine ends up as the crown once the pot is inverted.

name: Musakhan
clues: It was invented to celebrate the year's first pressing, and it uses that liquid with a generosity that shocks outsiders.
The flatbread underneath is baked on hot stones, and its dimples exist precisely to hold what soaks into it.
Roast poultry over bread saturated purple-red with a tart ground berry and a great quantity of onion.
The Palestinian dish of sumac-and-onion chicken roasted over taboon flatbread, drenched in olive oil.
fact: It is traditionally made at olive harvest, and the amount of fresh oil poured over is the measure of the host's generosity.

name: Muhammara
clues: Its name simply means reddened, and it comes from a city whose particular dried chilli is famous worldwide.
It arrives as part of the mezze spread, usually next to its paler chickpea neighbour.
A coarse, slightly gritty paste of charred sweet peppers and ground nuts, sweet-sour and gently hot.
The Aleppan dip of roasted red pepper and walnut with pomegranate molasses, eaten with flatbread.
fact: Breadcrumbs are the traditional binder, and the texture is meant to stay rough rather than being blended smooth.

name: Manakish
clues: Its name refers to the dents pressed into the dough by the baker's fingertips before it goes into the oven.
Families once carried their own trays to the neighbourhood oven in the morning; students now eat it rolled up on the way to class.
A flatbread baked with a paste of oil and a green herb-and-sumac blend, folded in half around cucumber and mint.
The Levantine breakfast flatbread topped with zaatar and olive oil, or with stretchy white cheese.
fact: The zaatar blend on top is a mix of dried thyme or hyssop, sesame seeds and sumac, and every family claims a different ratio.

name: Knafeh
clues: One West Bank city holds the record for the largest ever made, at over seventy metres long.
It is cut and served straight from a vast round tray, and eating it cold is considered a waste.
A layer of unsweetened brined cheese under a bright orange crust of shredded pastry, flooded with syrup while still hot.
The Levantine hot cheese dessert with a crisp orange topping, drenched in syrup and pistachios.
fact: Nablus is its spiritual home, and the local sheep's-milk cheese is desalted by soaking before it can be used.

name: Lahmacun
clues: Its Arabic name means meat with dough, and it is eaten rolled around a fistful of leaves rather than sliced.
It belongs to the south-east of its country and to Armenian and Syrian kitchens that claim it too.
A cracker-thin round baked in seconds under fierce heat, with a paper-thin smear of spiced mince across the top.
The Turkish flatbread spread with minced lamb and pepper paste, squeezed with lemon and rolled up with parsley.
fact: The meat layer must be spread almost translucently thin, which is why it cooks through in under two minutes.

name: İskender Kebab
clues: It is named after the nineteenth-century butcher who is credited with turning the roasting spit upright.
It comes from Bursa, and the family that invented it still trades on the name.
Sliced spit-roasted meat over cubes of bread, with tomato sauce and a ladle of foaming hot butter poured at the table.
The Bursa dish of döner lamb on bread with tomato sauce, yogurt and sizzling melted butter.
fact: İskender Efendi's innovation of the vertical spit in the 1860s is what made döner as we know it possible.

name: Menemen
clues: The great national argument about it concerns whether one particular allium belongs in it at all.
It arrives at the breakfast table in the same small two-handled copper pan it was cooked in.
Eggs stirred loosely into a base of softened peppers and tomato so it stays wet and spoonable, never set firm.
The Turkish breakfast of eggs cooked into stewed green peppers and tomato, eaten straight from the pan with bread.
fact: Purists insist onion has no place in it; adding onion is widely held to make it a different dish altogether.

name: Doro Wat
clues: Its foundation is an enormous quantity of one vegetable, cooked dry in a pan with no fat at all before anything else is added.
It is the dish that breaks the long fasts of the Orthodox calendar, and tradition allots twelve pieces of the bird.
A dark red, almost mahogany sauce built on a complex chilli blend and spiced clarified butter, with whole eggs sunk into it.
The Ethiopian chicken stew in berbere and spiced butter, served on a sour flatbread with boiled eggs.
fact: The onions are dry-cooked first to drive off water and collapse them into the sauce, which can take well over an hour.

name: Kitfo
clues: You are asked how you want it, and the traditional answer is the one that involves no cooking whatsoever.
It belongs to the Gurage people, and is often served with a dense bread fermented from the false banana plant.
Finely minced meat warmed only by spiced clarified butter, dressed with a fierce bird's-eye chilli powder.
The Ethiopian raw minced beef dish with spiced butter and mitmita, served with fresh curd cheese and greens.
fact: Ordering it leb leb means barely warmed through; yebesele means fully cooked, and purists consider that a different dish.

name: Bunny Chow
clues: Its name has nothing to do with rabbits; it most likely comes from the caste name of the Gujarati traders who sold it.
It was created under apartheid, when takeaway had to be sold to non-white customers through a hatch with no cutlery or plate.
A quarter or half of an unsliced white loaf, hollowed out and filled with curry, the removed crumb balanced on top as a lid.
The Durban street dish of curry served inside a hollowed-out loaf of bread.
fact: The plug of bread pulled out of the loaf is called the virgin, and it is used to mop up what soaks into the walls.

name: Bobotie
clues: Bay leaves are stood upright in its surface before baking, more for scent and looks than for flavour.
It comes from the Cape Malay community, descended from people brought to the Cape from Southeast Asia.
Mildly curried mince, sweetened with dried fruit and chutney, sealed under a savoury egg-and-milk topping that bakes into custard.
South Africa's baked spiced mince dish with a golden egg custard crust, served with yellow rice.
fact: It is usually served with turmeric-yellow rice studded with raisins, and the sweet-savoury balance is the point of the dish.

name: Thieboudienne
clues: The grain used is deliberately fractured, a legacy of colonial rice imports that turned out to suit the dish perfectly.
It is credited to a nineteenth-century cook from Saint-Louis and was inscribed by UNESCO in 2021.
Fish stuffed with a green herb paste, simmered with root vegetables, then the grain cooked in the same red broth.
Senegal's national one-pot of stuffed fish and vegetables with broken rice in tomato sauce.
fact: Penda Mbaye of Saint-Louis is the cook traditionally credited with creating it in the 1800s.

name: Waakye
clues: Dried red leaves are boiled with it purely for colour, turning everything a deep reddish brown.
It came south with Hausa traders, and is sold from a covered basin at the roadside, wrapped in leaves.
Grains and pulses cooked together, served with a spoonful of black chilli paste, grated cassava, spaghetti and egg.
Ghana's rice-and-beans breakfast, coloured with sorghum leaves and served with shito and gari.
fact: The dried sorghum leaf sheaths are alkaline as well as colouring, which also helps the beans soften.

name: Egusi Soup
clues: The ground seed at its heart comes from a gourd grown not for its flesh but for what is inside it.
It is eaten with a swallow — a stiff starch dough that is pinched, dipped and swallowed without chewing.
A thick orange-green stew that sets into soft curds as the ground seeds cook, rich with red palm oil and dried fish.
The West African stew of ground melon seeds with leafy greens, palm oil and assorted meats.
fact: The seeds are toasted and ground, then added in lumps so they steam into distinct curds rather than dissolving.
